source_read: PMC HTML (PMC6990973; JAMA Psychiatry 2020;77(3):246-255, published online 11 Dec 2019), saved plain text of the PMC article page read start to end: Key Points, abstract, Introduction, Methods (recruitment, procedures, measures, data analysis), Results (participants with Table 1, retention and adherence, Table 2 primary and secondary outcomes, methamphetamine use, sensitivity and as-treated analyses, beyond-threshold weeks and end-of-study abstinence, sexual risk with Table 3, craving, depression and sleep, adherence, safety), Discussion, Limitations, Conclusions, supplement list and reference list. Not available: Figure 1 (CONSORT) and Figure 2 (positivity by arm) are images; Supplement 1 (eTable with sensitivity-analysis estimates, eFigure), Supplement 2 (protocol) and Supplement 3 (data sharing) were not available; the saved text contains no Article Information block, so funding, conflict-of-interest disclosures, author contributions and the trial's dates of acceptance could not be read.

claims.overstatement: Slight, one word: 'non-depressed'. The trial excluded current major depression (Methods > Recruitment; Limitations), but it does not describe participants as non-depressed, and their baseline CES-D averaged 20.2 (SD 8.8), which on the standard 20-item scale lies above the usual screening threshold of 16 (the threshold is general knowledge, not stated in the paper; the paper cites a short-version reference and does not say which version it used). 'Without current major depression' matches the source. Minor: the 24-week net RR 0.75 (0.56-1.00, p = .05) sits under the verb 'lowered'; the claim prints its interval, so the borderline result is visible.
claims.note: Scope of this check: coffin_2020 covers the second trial only. The first trial's figures (RR 0.57, 0.35-0.93; raw final-visit positivity 44% vs 63%; editors' RR 0.71, 0.42-1.18) are not reported in this source, which says only that its authors' prior 12-week trial in 60 men who have sex with men showed significant reductions; those numbers must be checked against colfax_2011. Second-trial numbers recomputed: week-12 positive samples 25/38 = 65.8% vs 32/41 = 78.0%; week 24 20/32 = 62.5% (printed 63%) vs 29/39 = 74.4%; week 36 25/35 = 71.4% vs 37/42 = 88.1%; all match. Modelled RRs 0.67 (0.51-0.87), 0.75 (0.56-1.00), 0.73 (0.57-0.96) match Table 2 and the abstract. End-of-study abstinence 11/60 = 18.3% vs 5/60 = 8.3%; crude OR from these counts is 2.47 (0.80-7.61): the printed interval reproduces exactly, and the printed point estimate 2.50 is evidently rounded (the paper gives 2.50 for weeks 12, 24 and 36; week 36 recomputes to 2.51, 0.62-10.21). NNT 1/0.10 = 10 at weeks 12 and 24 and 1/0.067 = 15 at week 36, as printed. Drowsiness 18/60 = 30% vs 6/60 = 10% (no test reported). WisePill adherence means 38.5% vs 39.5% (week 12) and 28.1% vs 38.5% (week 24), all below 50%. Editors' rough check (not a reproduction of the model): the raw sample-level ratios are about 0.84 (week 12), 0.84 (week 24) and 0.81 (week 36); dividing by the baseline ratio of urine positivity (85% vs 75%, 1.13) gives 0.74, 0.74 and 0.72, close to the modelled 0.67, 0.75 and 0.73. The modelled effect is therefore largely the mirtazapine arm's larger fall from a higher starting point, which is what a divergence-of-trends model estimates but is worth knowing when the claim sets 66% vs 78% beside RR 0.67. 'Lowered the modelled weekly probability' fairly describes the GEE log-link RR (divergence of fitted trends after accounting for the fitted baseline difference, week 1 omitted). On independence: the source's Key Points call the two studies '2 independent randomized clinical trials', while the Introduction and Discussion describe the first as the authors' own earlier 12-week trial by the same group, and two authors of this trial (G. Colfax, G.-M. Santos) are the first two authors of the prior trial (reference 30). Shared investigators, group and population are thus documented here; shared site and analysis model are not described for the first trial in this source.

anchors.locator: Abstract (Design, Setting, and Participants; Exposures); Methods, 1st paragraph; Recruitment; Procedures, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, 1:1, August 2013 to September/October 2017, one outpatient research clinic in San Francisco. Eligible: ages 18-65, SCID DSM-IV-TR methamphetamine dependence, wish to cut down or stop, anal sex with men while using methamphetamine in the prior 6 months, methamphetamine-positive urine; cisgender men, transgender men and transgender women. Excluded: current major depression or other psychiatric condition precluding safe participation, recent non-permitted antidepressants, prior mirtazapine trial. Study conditions: mirtazapine 15 mg in week 1 then 30 mg daily to week 24, or matched placebo; 12 more weeks of follow-up off medication. Everyone had weekly urine tests and weekly manual-driven 30-minute counselling (CBT and motivational interviewing); drug dispensed in WisePill electronic containers; up to USD 595 compensation.

241 assessed, 120 randomized (60 per arm); most common exclusion psychotic disorder (n = 40). 115 cisgender men (95.8%) and 5 transgender women; no transgender men enrolled. Mean age 43.3 (SD 9.8); 51.7% living with HIV. Baseline CES-D mean 20.7 vs 19.8 (overall 20.2, SD 8.8). Use 5-7 days a week in past 4 weeks 51.7% in both arms; 1 day a week or less 11.7% vs 23.3%; craving 5.8 vs 4.7 (p = .08).

Primary outcome a repeated weekly indicator of methamphetamine-positive urine. Intent-to-treat GEE with log link and robust SEs; week-1 results omitted by prespecification; group-specific piecewise linear trends (weeks 2-12, 13-24, 25-36), treatment effect = divergence of the arms' fitted trends at 12, 24 and 36 weeks after accounting for the fitted baseline difference. Primary analysis assumes urine results missing completely at random given time and treatment. Powered (80%) to detect RR 0.81 for weeks 2-12, assuming 90%/85%/80% retention. Five sensitivity analyses prespecified.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (Primary outcomes, intent-to-treat, with footnotes b-c); Results > Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph; Abstract (Results)
anchors.extracted: Treatment effect at 12 weeks RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.51-0.87), p = .003; net effect at 24 weeks (end of medication) 0.75 (0.56-1.00), p = .05; net effect at 36 weeks (12 weeks after medication stopped) 0.73 (0.57-0.96), p = .02. Raw positive samples: week 12, 25 of 38 (66%) vs 32 of 41 (78%); week 24, 20 of 32 (63%) vs 29 of 39 (74%); week 36, 25 of 35 (71%) vs 37 of 42 (88%). Baseline positive urine 51/60 (85%) vs 45/60 (75%), p = .16.

anchors.locator: Results > Methamphetamine Use, 2nd paragraph; Sensitivity Analyses
anchors.extracted: Missing urine samples far above the planning assumptions: 41 of 120 (34%) at week 12, 49 (41%) at week 24, 43 (36%) at week 36, against 10%, 15% and 20% assumed. Sensitivity analyses including week 1, imputing missing samples as positive, and adjusting for baseline imbalances and correlates of missingness all favoured mirtazapine significantly (estimates only in the unavailable eTable); stratifying by baseline intensity of use showed no significant effect.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (beyond-threshold weeks; end-of-study abstinence, footnote f); Results > Number of Beyond-Threshold Weeks of Success; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: End-of-study abstinence (no use in the last 2 weeks before each evaluation point): 11/60 (18%) vs 5/60 (8%) at weeks 12 and 24, p = .11, OR 2.50 (0.80-7.61); 7/60 (12%) vs 3/60 (5%) at week 36, p = .19, OR 2.50 (0.62-10.20); NNT 10, 10, 15. Median beyond-threshold weeks of success 0 (IQR 0-0) in both arms at all three points. Authors: the reduction in use was modest overall and not significant on abstinence-based analyses.

anchors.locator: Results > Medication Adherence; Table 2 (adherence rows); Results > As-Treated Analyses
anchors.extracted: WisePill adherence mean 38.5% vs 39.5% at week 12 (p = .77) and 28.1% vs 38.5% at week 24 (p = .59); self-report 44.3% vs 46.1% and 38.8% vs 37.5%; at least 50% of doses taken by 37% vs 35% (week 12) and 22% vs 20% (week 24). As-treated, upper half of adherence: cumulative adherence RR 0.70 (0.38-1.28) at 12 weeks and 0.69 (0.50-0.95) at 24 weeks; past-week adherence 0.64 (0.36-1.13) and 0.73 (0.50-1.08).

Fatigue or drowsiness 18 (30%) on mirtazapine vs 6 (10%) on placebo; unintentional weight gain 4 (7%) vs 1 (2%); increased appetite 1 vs 1. Nine serious adverse events reported, none judged drug-related (the text describes eight: in the mirtazapine arm one death from unintentional opioid overdose and hospitalisations for deep venous thrombosis, heart failure and soft-tissue infection; in the placebo arm four hospitalisations). No statistical comparison of adverse events.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Key Points (Findings, Meaning); author list; reference 30
anchors.extracted: The first trial is described as the authors' own prior 12-week trial in 60 men who have sex with men (reference 30: Colfax, Santos, Das et al., 2011), and this trial as a replication and expansion of it. Colfax and G.-M. Santos are authors of both trials. The Key Points nonetheless call them two independent randomized clinical trials. This source gives no first-trial effect sizes and does not describe its site or analysis model.

Weekly visits completed 69% vs 63%; dropouts 20 (33%) vs 13 (22%), p = .21; final-visit completion 38 vs 42 participants. Blinding check at week 24: 46% vs 49% guessed their arm correctly. Limitations: results may not generalise beyond cisgender men and transgender women who have sex with men; people with major depression not enrolled; many secondary outcomes at several time points without correction for multiple comparisons.

key_findings.correction: Counts are in the Results text (Figure 2 itself is an image). Editors' risk differences recomputed: -12.3 (-32.0 to 7.4), -11.9 (-33.5 to 9.8), -16.7 (-34.6 to 1.2); ratios 0.84, 0.84, 0.81.

Two small points: the paper defines end-of-study abstinence as abstinence in the last 2 weeks before each evaluation point and does not say how missing urines were handled, so 'no positive urine' is the card's paraphrase; and the printed OR 2.50 for weeks 12 and 24 is rounded, since the counts give a crude OR of 2.47 whose interval (0.80-7.61) matches the printed one exactly (week 36: 2.51, 0.62-10.21). Table 2 gives P = .72 for beyond-threshold weeks at week 36, the text P = .71.

The card's list of non-significant measures omits condomless insertive anal sex with serodiscordant partners (RR 0.56, 0.24-1.31, P = .18 at 24 weeks); its analysis field does count three non-significant measures.
Editors' calculation reproduces: risk difference 20.0 points (6.1 to 33.9), Fisher's exact two-sided p = 0.011.

NOT CHECKED rather than absent: this finding comes from the ClinicalTrials.gov record, which I could not open in this session (no web access). The article itself prints only the registration number NCT01888835 (Abstract, Trial Registration) and says the analysis model was prespecified with the protocol in Supplement 2 (not available). The registry dates, outcome history and the absence of posted results need a second check by someone with web access.

reporting_issues.note: The printed 48% and 53% equal 38/80 and 42/80, not 38/60 and 42/60; also, 38 completers plus 20 dropouts (58) and 42 plus 13 (55) do not account for all 60 per arm, so 'completion' and 'dropout' are defined differently or some participants were neither.
Fisher's exact test for 43/60 vs 43/60 gives p = 1.00; P = .28 is the value printed for weekly visit completion (69% vs 63%) in the same paragraph, so a copied value is likely.

Duplication confirmed (placebo week 24 = mirtazapine week 12 = 38.5%, SD 27.0). The editors' P range depends on the n assumed: a normal approximation gives p about .06 with 43 per arm (the week-24 attenders) and about .11 with 30 per arm (Wilcoxon was used); either way far from .59. Suggest 'P of roughly .04 to .11' rather than '.03 to .06'. The consequence's remark about secondary sources is borne out: siefried_2020 (Discussion > Reduction in Use) quotes adherence as '28.1-39.5%' across the two arms.

Footnotes b and c read as stated. Adding to the ambiguity, the as-treated rows are labelled '24 wk, net of any difference from weeks 2-12', which points to the period-increment reading, while the Data Analysis section (effects defined as the divergence of the arms' trends at each time point after allowing for the fitted baseline difference) and the raw-data check (0.74 and 0.72, reproduced) point to the cumulative reading.
Results text gives 1.2 points lower (0.02 to 2.3), P = .06, an interval that would exclude zero; Table 2 gives -1.15 (-2.33 to 0.02). The text's lower limit should evidently be -0.02.

NOT CHECKED on the registry side (ClinicalTrials.gov not accessible in this session). Article side confirmed: ages 18 to 65, anal sex with men while using methamphetamine within the prior 6 months, and five named SSRIs permitted (Methods > Recruitment); four participants (3%) were taking SSRIs (Sensitivity Analyses).

Key Points wording confirmed. From this source alone the shared authorship is visible for Colfax and G.-M. Santos only (reference 30 lists Colfax, Santos, Das et al.); the other three shared authors, the shared site, counselling and analysis model come from the 2011 paper and are not checkable here. Related: the Introduction describes the prior trial as '60 men who have sex with men and were treated with mirtazapine', which can be misread as 60 people on mirtazapine; the first trial's arm sizes should be taken from colfax_2011. The card's timeline entry on Siefried 2020 is confirmed from my reading of that review: it describes this trial in its Discussion as published by the same group after its search and as a replication, and does not include it among its 43 trials.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 domain judgments follow from the article: concealed off-site allocation and identical over-encapsulation (randomization low; the 85% vs 75% baseline positivity is compatible with chance); double-blind with intention-to-treat and a blinding check (deviations low); objective urine outcome (measurement low); 34-41% missing urines, more dropout on mirtazapine and a missing-completely-at-random primary analysis, with the positive-imputation sensitivity analysis only described in words (missing data some concerns, which I would not raise to high given that analysis reportedly stayed significant). Overall some concerns follows. One limit of my check: the 'selection of the reported result: low' judgment rests partly on the registry history, which I could not open; the article does say the model was prespecified, gives the registration number and puts the protocol in a supplement I could not read.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's content is right, but I would rate the gap 'substantial' rather than 'minor'. The Key Points, the part most often quoted, say mirtazapine is the first medication to show efficacy for methamphetamine use disorder in two independent trials (same team and population; abstinence not significantly different in this trial and most samples stayed positive) and that the sexual-risk reductions were consistent with the previous study, which the paper's own Discussion contradicts ('In contrast with the original study', with reductions only at 24 weeks, 3 of 6 measures at P = .04, no multiplicity correction). The Results text also calls the 24-week decline significant (RR 0.75, 0.56-1.00, P = .05). The Discussion and Limitations are measured, so the gap is between the body and the Key Points/abstract. Senior-author call.

missed: Results > Methamphetamine Use, 1st paragraph and the abstract describe the 24-week effect as a significant decline or a reduction, although its interval reaches 1.00 (P = .05); the card records the interval but not this wording, which matters for any claim that 'lowered' use at 24 weeks.

Overall weekly-visit completion is given as mean 66% with SD 47%, while the arm SDs are 32% and 31%; 47% is the SD of a binary visit indicator at 66% (computed over visits, not participants), so the overall SD is on a different basis from the arm SDs. Minor.

Funding and conflict-of-interest details on the card (NIH R01DA034527, NIDA R01DA031678; disclosures) could not be checked: the saved PMC text has no Article Information block. Treat these card fields as single-reader.
